title: Calendar Counter
context: Grade 4, and the recap topic, where the chapter moves from the clock to the calendar. An adult sees a calendar being read, which every classroom wall allows. What is actually being settled is three rules the page states badly or not at all. A year is fifty-two weeks and one day, three hundred and sixty-five days in all. A year divisible by four is a leap year, except a century year not divisible by four hundred, so 1900 was not a leap year and 2000 was. And a count of the days between two dates has no answer until it is decided whether the first day and the last day count. The page changes that from one example to the next without saying so.

writeup.why: Know the days in each month and in a year, and decide whether a year is a leap year. Count the days between two dates with each end decided first, and write a date in short form.
writeup.look: A wall of twelve month cards under a year dial, a rack of month bars and a weeks ruler, a day counter with two end switches, and a date writer.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Calendar Counter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the months sorted, the gate's questions answered, the days counted or the slots filled against what this phase holds, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each settles and the second fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The year dial stands at the top left of the working area, 240 by 52 at 76,214, reading the year in ink and starting at 2026. The calendar wall stands under it, 640 by 452 at 76,274: the twelve month cards of the dialled year in three rows of four, each card 152 by 144 with its month's name, the columns S M T W T F S, and its dates laid out as the calendar in use today lays out that year, its first day under the right weekday. The right-hand column, 400 wide from 740, holds a different piece on each phase. On the first, the month rack, 400 by 190 at 740,214, has three olive bars, for months of thirty-one days, months of thirty days and February, and the year bar under them adds the twelve months into one total. The weeks ruler under the rack, 400 by 250 at 740,420, lays the year's days out in rows of seven, fifty-two full rows in four blocks of thirteen, and the days left over stand after them in yellow outlined in near-black: one in a year of three hundred and sixty-five days and two in a leap year. On the second, the leap year gate, 400 by 300 at 740,214, asks three questions in order, each a near-black box with a yes path and a no path: is the year divisible by four, is it a century year, and is it divisible by four hundred. The path the dialled year takes lights, and a leap year grows a twenty-ninth of February on the wall in yellow outlined in near-black. On the third, the two end switches, 400 by 80 at 740,214, one for whether the first day counts and one for whether the last day counts, must both be set before the day counter under them, 400 by 200 at 740,310, will light. It then counts month by month, writing the days in the first month, any whole months, and the days in the last month, while the counted days on the wall fill in green one by one and a day left out is outlined only, at full strength. The holiday shelf, 400 by 110 at 740,524, holds cards that each show a holiday with its date. On the fourth, the date writer, 400 by 200 at 740,214, has two-place slots for the day and the month and a four-place slot for the year, day first, and a switch under them for dots, slashes or dashes. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve keys three across, the ten digits and two keys that clear and go back, with a word pad of the months and the weekdays over it where a month or a day is asked for, and yes and no keys on the second phase. On the third phase the answer slot will not open until both end switches are set, and on the fourth it holds the day, the month and the year in places of their own. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The hour hand, every hour tile and hour cell, the hours column, and the hours of a time the stage splits into hours and minutes are vermilion. The minute hand, every minute tile and minute cell, the minutes column and the minutes of a split time are deep blue. The second hand, every second cell and the seconds column are reddish purple. The a.m. half of the day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue on every strip, timeline and track, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber, so the label changes where the colour does. Time counted between a start and an end, every hop and total on a track, and the days counted between two dates are green. An hour or a minute carried or broken, with the digits it strikes and rewrites, is wine. A calendar day, week or year picked out or ticked, a month on its bar and a day tile are olive. The days left over beyond whole weeks, and the twenty-ninth of February in a leap year, are yellow outlined in near-black. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every clock rim, minute mark, clock number, hub, rule, tick, post, bracket, guide line and panel edge is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because an hour hand is told from a minute hand by its length, a column by its heading, a half of the day by its label, and a counted day from one left out by being filled rather than outlined, before any of them is told by a colour. A figure that goes down by one is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. Every day count on this stage shows which of its ends it counts: a counted day is filled and a day left out is outlined only, at full strength and never hidden. The holiday shelf gives the date of each holiday it holds, and the wall draws each dialled year as the calendar in use today lays it out.
writeup.finish: The card shows the wall with the child's last count lit day by day, the two end switches as they set them, and the dates they wrote in short form.

phases.win: the year bar reads three hundred and sixty-five, and the weeks ruler shows full rows of seven with one day over
phases.does: sorts the months onto their bars, adds the year on the year bar, lays the weeks ruler along it, then finds a chosen weekday in a month
phases.goal: four months have thirty days, seven have thirty-one and February twenty-eight, three hundred and sixty-five days in all, which is fifty-two weeks and one day
phases.says: Which months have thirty days? Now add all twelve. How many whole weeks is that, and what is left?
phases.check: Away from the screen: how many days do April, May and June have together?
phases.feels: the months do not share one length, and the year does not fill its weeks exactly
phases.hands: Hang a real calendar for this year and have groups list the months with thirty days, the months with thirty-one, and February. Add the three groups on the board, then count the year's days off in sevens and ask what is left over.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which bar does this month go on? Second rung, the phase's: how many days are left after the full weeks? Third rung: the wall is cut to three months, one quarter of the year, and the child sorts and adds them before the whole year comes back. The pad and the word pad stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: a year sounds like a whole number of weeks, and a single day left over is too small to notice.
wrong.move: calls a year of three hundred and sixty-five days exactly fifty-two weeks, one day short of its length.
wrong.screen: the weeks ruler lays the year bar's three hundred and sixty-five days out in rows of seven, and fifty-two full rows fill, three hundred and sixty-four days, with one yellow day standing alone after them. The child's answer stays in the slot beside the ruler, nothing marked.

wrong.why: from January to July, with February left aside, the months do go long and short in turn, so the pattern looks as if it runs on.
wrong.move: gives August thirty days, taking the months to go thirty-one, thirty, thirty-one, thirty all through the year.
wrong.screen: August's card slides onto the thirty-one bar, and its dates on the wall run to the thirty-first. July and August stand side by side on that bar, two months in a row with thirty-one days each, and the child's thirty stays in the slot.

phases.screen: the wall of twelve month cards for 2026 and the empty month rack
phases.soWhat: A year of three hundred and sixty-five days is fifty-two weeks and one day, and a leap year is fifty-two weeks and two days, one day more.
phases.concept: Days in the months and the year

phases.win: February grows a twenty-ninth day for each leap year, the year bar reads three hundred and sixty-six, and a century year that fails the last question stays at twenty-eight
phases.does: dials a year, runs it through the three questions of the gate in order, and watches February
phases.goal: a year divisible by four is a leap year, except a century year not divisible by four hundred; a leap year has twenty-nine days in February
phases.says: Is the year divisible by four? Is it a century year? If it is, ask about four hundred.
phases.check: Was 1904 a leap year? Was 1900? Say which questions each one passed.
phases.feels: four gives the rule, a century year breaks it, and four hundred mends it again
phases.hands: Say that the earth takes about three hundred and sixty-five and a quarter days to go round the sun, which is why some years have a twenty-ninth of February. Then write five years on the board, 2024, 2025, 1900, 2000 and 2100, and for each ask the three questions in order: is it divisible by four, is it a century year, and if it is, is it divisible by four hundred. Ask which of the five had, or will have, a twenty-ninth of February.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: is the year divisible by four? Second rung, the phase's: is it a century year, and if it is, is it divisible by four hundred? Third rung: the dial is cut to a year that is not a century year, and the child runs it through the first question before the century year comes back. The yes and no keys stay open.

wrong.why: the rule about four is the one a child meets first, and 1700 passes it.
wrong.move: calls 1700 a leap year because it is divisible by four, stopping at the first question.
wrong.screen: the gate takes 1700 through all three questions: yes at divisible by four, yes at century year, and no at divisible by four hundred, and the no path lights. February on the wall stays at twenty-eight days and the year bar at three hundred and sixty-five, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the part about century years is heard last, and the part about four hundred is easy to drop.
wrong.move: calls 1600 not a leap year because it is a century year, as if every century year were left out.
wrong.screen: the gate takes 1600 on past the century question to the last one, divisible by four hundred, where it answers yes, and the yes path lights. February on the wall grows a twenty-ninth day in yellow, the year bar reads three hundred and sixty-six, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: the year dial and the leap year gate, with February on the wall showing twenty-eight days
phases.soWhat: A year divisible by four is a leap year, except a century year not divisible by four hundred. A leap year has twenty-nine days in February.

phases.win: the counted days light on the wall, the parts are written month by month, and they add to the total
phases.does: sets whether the first day counts and whether the last day counts, then counts the days left in the first month, any whole months, and the days in the last month
phases.goal: before counting the days between two dates, decide whether the first day and the last day count, then count month by month
phases.says: Before you count, does the first day count? Does the last day count?
phases.check: How many days are there from 25 June to 10 July, counting both dates?
phases.feels: each end is a decision, and the count moves by one each time an end is turned in or out
phases.hands: Choose a class event on a real calendar, and before anyone counts the days to it, have the class decide whether today counts and whether the event day counts. Count once with each choice and write the answers side by side, so everyone sees the count move by one for each end.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: does the first day count, and does the last? Second rung, the phase's: how many days are counted in the first month? Third rung: the dates are cut to two in the same month, and the child counts them with both switches set before the longer count comes back. The pad stays open, and the answer slot opens once both switches are set.

wrong.why: taking the first date from the month's days and adding the last date is a quick way through two months, and it quietly counts the last day in.
wrong.move: takes eighteen from thirty for September and adds seven for October, which counts 7 October, and answers nineteen days between 18 September and 7 October, not counting either date.
wrong.screen: the counter stays dark until both end switches are set to leave the ends out. It then fills in green the twelve days from 19 to 30 September and the six days from 1 to 6 October, and 7 October stands outlined only, not counted. The parts are written twelve and six, eighteen in all, and the child's nineteen stays in the slot beside them.

wrong.why: taking the first date away is the move that works when the first date is left out, and here it counts.
wrong.move: takes twelve from thirty for November, which leaves out 12 November, and answers twenty-one days from 12 November to 3 December, counting both dates.
wrong.screen: the first end switch reads counted, and 12 November fills in green on the wall with the eighteen days after it, nineteen in November. The three days of December fill after them, and the parts are written nineteen and three, twenty-two in all, beside the child's twenty-one in the slot.

wrong.why: adding a number of days to a date is a quick way to move along a calendar, and it leaves the first day out of the count.
wrong.move: adds sixteen to 22 March and writes 7 April as the last day of a sixteen-day tournament that counts 22 March as its first day.
wrong.screen: the first end switch reads counted, 22 March fills in green as day one, and the days fill on, ten in March and six in April, the sixteenth landing on 6 April. 7 April stands outlined only, the day after, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: two dates flagged on the wall, with both end switches unset and the day counter waiting
phases.soWhat: Decide whether each end counts before counting, then count month by month.

phases.win: the date settles in short form, and the same date shows with dots, with slashes and with dashes
phases.does: fills the day and the month with two digits each and the year with four, then switches between dots, slashes and dashes
phases.goal: a date in short form is the day, the month and the year in figures, day first, with two digits for the day and the month and four for the year
phases.says: Day first, then the month, then the year. How many digits does each one take?
phases.check: Write 5 September 2026 in short form, with dots and then with slashes.
phases.feels: the short form keeps one order, day, then month, then year, and fills every place
phases.hands: Write today's date in words on the board, and have the class write it in short form with the day first, two digits for the day and the month and four for the year. Then show the same date written month first, as some countries do, and ask which day it would be read as here.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which comes first in the short form? Second rung, the phase's: how many digits do the day and the month each take? Third rung: the writer is cut to a date whose day and month already have two digits, and the child writes it before the shorter numbers come back. The pad stays open.

wrong.why: some screens and calendars show the month first, and a date said aloud as January the third puts the month first.
wrong.move: writes the month first, 01.03.2027 for 3 January 2027, which reads as 1 March.
wrong.screen: the date writer's slots are labelled day, month and year in order, and the child's digits are read back through them: day one, month three, 1 March 2027, and that date lights on the wall two months on from 3 January. The digits are then set day first, 03.01.2027, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: three and one are single digits, and a nought in front of a number seems to add nothing.
wrong.move: drops the noughts and writes 3.1.2027 for 3 January 2027.
wrong.screen: the day and month slots of the date writer each show both places drawn, and their empty first places light until a nought fills each. The same date then shows with dots, slashes and dashes, 03.01.2027, 03/01/2027 and 03-01-2027, and the child's answer stays in the slot beside it.

phases.screen: a date written in words, and the date writer's three empty slots
phases.soWhat: A date in short form is the day, the month and the year in figures, day first, with two digits for the day and the month.
phases.concept: Writing a date in short form

writeup.delight: The first phase, when the year dial is turned on by one. The day left over on the weeks ruler lifts off in yellow and slides across the wall, and each month card's dates move one column to the right, so the first of January moves from a Thursday in 2026 to a Friday in 2027. Turned on from 2028, a leap year, two days lift off, and the first of January moves two columns, from a Saturday in 2028 to a Monday in 2029. It can be turned as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the wall shows the twelve month cards of 2026, the year of the chapter's printed calendar, and the month rack beside it is empty. On the second the year dial and the leap year gate stand at the right, with February on the wall showing twenty-eight days. On the third two dates are flagged on the wall, both end switches are unset, and the day counter is dark. On the fourth a date written in words stands above the date writer's three empty slots. The running count at the top left holds the months sorted, the gate's questions answered, the days counted or the slots filled against what this phase holds, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: January's card, or the dial, or the first end switch, or the day slot, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how many days are in this year. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any year on the dial, the whole calendar wall, the month rack, the weeks ruler, the leap year gate, the day counter, the holiday shelf and the date writer all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.

voiceLines: A wall of twelve months and a year dial. How many days are in this year?
Which months have thirty days? Now add all twelve. How many whole weeks is that, and what is left?
Is the year divisible by four? Is it a century year? If it is, ask about four hundred.
Before you count, does the first day count? Does the last day count?
Day first, then the month, then the year. How many digits does each one take?
A new question. Find the month on the wall before you count anything.
Free play. Any year on the dial, with the rack, the ruler, the gate, the counter and the date writer open.
Decide both ends first, then count month by month.
Months sorted, years run through the whole rule, counts begun with both ends decided, and dates written day first.

observations.soWhat: A year of three hundred and sixty-five days is fifty-two weeks and one day, and a leap year is fifty-two weeks and two days, one day more.
observations.observe: The year bar read three hundred and sixty-five, and the weeks ruler filled fifty-two rows of seven with one day over.

observations.why: A year divisible by four is a leap year, except a century year not divisible by four hundred, and the gate asks those questions in that order.
observations.soWhat: A year divisible by four is a leap year, except a century year not divisible by four hundred. A leap year has twenty-nine days in February.
observations.observe: February grew a twenty-ninth day for the years that passed the gate, and a century year that failed the last question kept twenty-eight.

observations.why: Whether each end counts changes the number of days by one for that end, so the count has no answer until both are decided.
observations.soWhat: Decide whether each end counts before counting, then count month by month.
observations.observe: The counter would not light until both switches were set, and the answer changed by one when a switch was turned.

observations.why: The short form writes the day, the month and the year in that order, and a nought fills an empty first place.

source_tool.description: A calendar wall fills the working area with the twelve month cards of one year, each a grid with the columns S M T W T F S. A year dial above it starts at 2026, the year of the chapter's printed calendar. A month rack beside the wall has three bars, for months of thirty-one days, months of thirty days and February, and a year bar adds the twelve months into one total. A weeks ruler lays the year's days out in rows of seven, so a year of three hundred and sixty-five days is seen as fifty-two weeks and one day. In a leap year two days are left over instead of one. A leap year gate takes the year on the dial through three questions in order: is it divisible by four, is it a century year, and is it divisible by four hundred. A leap year grows a twenty-ninth of February on the wall. A day counter takes a first date and a last date and will not count until two end switches are set. One says whether the first day counts and one whether the last day counts. It then counts month by month, the days in the first month, any whole months, and the days in the last month, lighting each counted day. A holiday shelf holds cards that each show a holiday with its date. A date writer has slots for the day, the month and the year, and a switch for dots, slashes or dashes.
source_tool.art_direction: A wall calendar and a year dial / Picture book

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a clock face with sixty marks, a strip of the day from one midnight to the next, a ladder of units with tiles, the page's own timeline, a column frame, a time track with flags and a hopper, and a wall of month cards.

Every clock is drawn exactly. The minute hand turns six degrees a minute and points exactly at a minute mark, and the hour hand turns thirty degrees an hour and half a degree a minute, so it sits exactly where the time puts it and never on a number except at the hour.

The minute hand is always the longer hand and the hour hand the shorter, and a second hand, where there is one, is the thinnest. A clock face always shows all twelve numbers and all sixty marks, with a longer mark at each number.
A time in figures is written with a colon and a.m. or p.m., as 4:40 p.m., and a 24-hour time as four digits and the word hours, as 1615 hours. Twelve o'clock is written 12 noon or 12 midnight.
Noon and midnight are drawn as posts wherever a strip, a timeline or a track crosses them, and a.m. changes to p.m., or back, only at a post.
A column of time carries at sixty. A carried or broken hour or minute is drawn as sixty cells in six rows of ten, never as ten or as a hundred.
A month card is the real month of the year shown, with its first day under the right weekday and the right number of days, as the calendar in use today lays out that year.
Every day count shows which of its ends it counts. A day that is counted is filled, and a day that is left out is outlined only, at full strength and never hidden.
Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
A hand, a column, a flag or a day is told apart by its shape, its label and its place first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a digit, a tile, a cell or a day the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The hour hand, an hour tile, an hours column and the hours of a time split into hours and minutes are vermilion. The minute hand and every minute are deep blue, and the second hand and every second are reddish purple, following the page, whose hour hand is red and whose second hand is a thin pink. The a.m. half of the day, midnight to noon, is sky blue on every strip, timeline and track, and the p.m. half is amber, so the label changes where the colour does. Time counted between a start and an end, every hop and total on the duration track, and the days counted between two dates are green. An hour or a minute carried or broken, with the digits it strikes and rewrites, is wine. A calendar day, week or year picked out or ticked, a month on its bar and a day tile on the ladder are olive. The days left over beyond whole weeks, and the twenty-ninth of February in a leap year, are yellow outlined in near-black. Every clock rim, minute mark, number, hub, rule, tick, post, bracket and guide line is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because an hour hand is told from a minute hand by its length, a column by its heading, a half of the day by its label, and a counted day from one left out by being filled rather than outlined.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Decide both ends first, then count month by month.
voice.onNext: A new question. Find the month on the wall before you count anything.
voice.opening: A wall of twelve months and a year dial. How many days are in this year?
voice.onFinish: Months sorted, years run through the whole rule, counts begun with both ends decided, and dates written day first.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any year on the dial, with the rack, the ruler, the gate, the counter and the date writer open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Days in the months and the year
Writing a date in short form

placement.where: After groups have found the third Saturday of a month on a real calendar for this year, and counted the days to the next class event with both ends decided first. The tool is what refuses to count until both ends are decided, and what runs any year through the whole leap year rule, which one printed calendar cannot do.

answer_key.rule: April, June, September and November have thirty days; January, March, May, July, August, October and December have thirty-one; February has twenty-eight, or twenty-nine in a leap year. A year that is not a leap year has three hundred and sixty-five days, which is fifty-two weeks and one day, and a leap year has three hundred and sixty-six. The earth takes about three hundred and sixty-five and a quarter days to go round the sun. A year divisible by four is a leap year, except a century year not divisible by four hundred: 1900 was not a leap year, and 2000 was. Before counting the days between two dates, decide whether each end counts, then count month by month. A date in short form is the day, the month and the year in figures, day first, as in 03.01.2027, and dots, slashes or dashes may separate them.
answer_key.wrong: The counter runs again with both end switches read aloud first, and each counted day lights on the wall as it is counted, month by month. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: A week is 7 days, and 52 weeks are 52 times 7, which is 364 days.
So the year is fifty-two weeks and one day, not a whole number of weeks.
items.question: A year that is not a leap year has 365 days. How many whole weeks is that, and how many days are left over?
items.checkpoint: A year of 365 days is fifty-two weeks and one day, and a leap year has one day more.
items.misconception: Saying a year is exactly fifty-two weeks, which would be only 364 days.

steps: 1996 is divisible by four and is not a century year, so it was a leap year.
1700 is divisible by four, but it is a century year not divisible by four hundred, so it was not a leap year.
1600 is a century year that is divisible by four hundred, so it was a leap year.
items.answer: 1996 and 1600 were leap years, and 1700 was not
items.question: Which of these years were leap years: 1996, 1700 and 1600?
items.checkpoint: A year divisible by four is a leap year, except a century year not divisible by four hundred.
items.misconception: Calling 1700 a leap year because it is divisible by four, and leaving out the century rule.

steps: Neither end counts, so start on 19 September and stop on 6 October.
From 19 to 30 September is 12 days, because September has 30 days and the first 18 are left out.
From 1 to 6 October is 6 days, and 12 and 6 make 18 days.
items.question: How many days are there between 18 September and 7 October, not counting either date?
items.checkpoint: Decide whether each end counts before counting, then count month by month.
items.misconception: Taking 18 from 30 and then adding 7, which counts 7 October when it should be left out, and answering 19.

steps: The day comes first, and 3 is written with two digits: 03.
January is the first month, so the month is 01.
The year is written in full, 2027, which gives 03.01.2027.
items.answer: 03.01.2027, which can also be written 03/01/2027 or 03-01-2027
items.question: Write 3 January 2027 in short form.
items.checkpoint: A short date is the day, the month and the year in figures, day first, with two digits for the day and the month.
items.misconception: Writing the month first, 01.03.2027, which reads as 1 March, or dropping the noughts and writing 3.1.2027.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: How many days does June have, and how many does August have?
items.final_answer: June has 30 days and August has 31

items.question: How many days does February have in 2028, and why?
items.final_answer: 29 days, because 2028 is divisible by four and is not a century year, so it is a leap year

items.question: 1 March 2026 is a Sunday. On which date is the third Saturday of March 2026?
items.final_answer: 21 March 2026. The first Saturday is 7 March, and two more weeks bring it to 14 March and then 21 March

items.question: Was 1800 a leap year?
items.final_answer: No. 1800 is divisible by four, but it is a century year not divisible by four hundred

items.question: How many days are there from 12 November to 3 December, counting both dates?
items.final_answer: 22 days: 19 days from 12 to 30 November, and 3 days from 1 to 3 December

items.question: Independence Day is on 15 August, and a school's sports day is on 2 September. How many days are there between them, not counting either day?
items.final_answer: 17 days: 16 days from 16 to 31 August, and 1 more day, 1 September

items.question: A tournament starts on 22 March and runs for 16 days, with the first day counted as day one. On which date is its last day? Play runs each day from 9:55 a.m. to 1:35 p.m. How long is that?
items.final_answer: Its last day is 6 April: 10 days from 22 to 31 March and 6 days in April. Play lasts 3 hours 40 minutes a day: count on to 12 noon, 2 hours 5 minutes, then 1 hour 35 minutes more

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: shows the twelve month cards of the year on the dial, each with the columns S M T W T F S
sets the year, starting at 2026, the year of the chapter's printed calendar
sorts the months onto bars of thirty-one days, thirty days and February
lays the year's days out in rows of seven and shows the days left over
asks divisible by four, then century year, then divisible by four hundred
say whether the first day and the last day count, and must both be set before a count
counts month by month between two dates, lighting each counted day
holds cards that each show a holiday with its date

teaching_notes: Use a real calendar for this year before the tool is opened. Have the class find the third Saturday of a month and count the days to a class event, saying first whether today and the event day count. The opening page asks for the date of the third Saturday in July this year and names no year. On the chapter's own printed calendar, for 2026, July begins on a Wednesday and its Saturdays fall on the fourth, eleventh, eighteenth and twenty-fifth. So the answer for 2026 is the eighteenth of July; say which year you are using. The page says a year is twelve months or fifty-two weeks; say fifty-two weeks and one day. Its leap year rules are a flat rule and an exception that breaks it, and they never say that a century year divisible by four hundred is a leap year. State the rule whole every time: a year divisible by four is a leap year, except a century year not divisible by four hundred. The worked day counts change which ends they count from one example to the next, so ask about both ends before every count. The exercise and the On Your Own box need holiday dates the chapter never gives. Republic Day is 26 January, Independence Day 15 August, Teacher's Day 5 September, Children's Day 14 November and Christmas Day 25 December. One exercise does not say whether the day of leaving is one of the fifty-four days of a visit. It is 2 July if it is, and 3 July, the book's answer, if it is not. Accept any day-first short form of a date, with dots, slashes or dashes. The closing page asks for finishing dates and daily durations. Its four find-outs about the pool, the races and a venue need facts no page gives, so this plan does not answer them. The six self-assessment statements say nothing about counting days or writing dates, so add both when the class ticks the list, and make flashcards for the eleven vocabulary words.
generation_prompt: Build a calendar tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A wall of twelve month cards fills most of the working area, each a grid headed S M T W T F S. The cards show the year on the year dial above them. The dial starts at 2026, and every year dialled is laid out by the calendar in use today. A month rack beside the wall has bars for months of thirty-one days, thirty days and February, and a year bar adds the twelve months into one total. A weeks ruler lays the year's days out in rows of seven and shows the days left over. One is left in a year of three hundred and sixty-five days, and two in a leap year. A leap year gate takes the dialled year through three questions in order, divisible by four, a century year, divisible by four hundred, lighting the path taken. February on the wall grows a twenty-ninth day only for a leap year. A day counter takes a first and a last date and stays unlit until two end switches are set, one for whether the first day counts and one for the last. It then counts month by month, writing each month's part and lighting each counted day, with any day left out outlined only. A holiday shelf holds cards each showing a holiday and its date. A date writer has two-digit slots for the day and the month and a four-digit slot for the year, day first, with a switch for dots, slashes or dashes. A list of six can-do statements and a word pad of the chapter's eleven vocabulary words sit under the slot. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Sort the months by their days. Add the year and lay out the weeks. Run the year through the leap year gate. Before counting days, decide both ends. Write the day, then the month, then the year.
